title: Gunn v. Minton (2013)
summary: The patent-related malpractice claim remained a state-court matter because the embedded patent issue did not have the necessary significance to the federal system.
notes:
A necessary federal issue is only one part of the test. Grable’s system-wide concern with federal tax collection differs from the case-specific malpractice counterfactual here.

Minton's TEXCEN trading-software patent was invalidated under the on-sale bar because he had leased the system more than a year before applying; Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a unanimous Court, restating the Grable inquiry as whether the federal issue is (1) necessarily raised, (2) actually disputed, (3) substantial, and (4) capable of federal resolution without disrupting the federal-state balance approved by Congress.

sections.Parties: Minton sued his former attorney Gunn after losing a federal patent case.
sections.Material Facts: Minton’s patent had been held invalid. In the later malpractice action, he contended that his lawyers failed to raise an experimental-use argument that would have avoided that result. Success therefore required deciding whether the omitted argument would have changed the earlier case. That hypothetical decision could affect malpractice liability, but it would not reopen or change the actual patent judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The Texas Supreme Court held that the malpractice action belonged in federal court. The Supreme Court of the United States reversed, applying the same arising-under framework used for §§ 1331 and 1338.
sections.Issue: Did the necessary patent issue in this state-law malpractice claim create exclusive federal patent jurisdiction?
sections.Holding: No. Although the issue was necessary and disputed, it lacked the required substantiality to the federal system and did not justify disturbing the normal state role.
sections.Reasoning: The Court distinguished the importance of an issue to the litigants from its importance to the federal legal system. The malpractice inquiry was backward-looking and hypothetical. A state court’s answer would not alter the prior federal judgment, govern future patent cases as binding precedent, or change the actual validity of the patent. Federal courts retained authority to decide patent law for themselves. States also have a substantial interest in regulating the professional obligations of lawyers. Those considerations prevented the embedded patent question from converting this ordinary malpractice controversy into a federal case.

learning.why: The patent-related malpractice claim remained a state-court matter because the embedded patent issue did not have the necessary significance to the federal system.

topics.cp-embedded-question: The malpractice claim required a hypothetical patent determination. The backward-looking patent issue was not substantial to the federal system as a whole.
topics.cp-federalism: State regulation of lawyers weighed against transferring ordinary malpractice claims to exclusive federal jurisdiction.
topics.cp-federal-question: Gunn restates the Grable four-part test for § 1331 and § 1338 arising-under jurisdiction.
